prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay on whether it is wrong to eat animals
raw:
The first pig I ever killed myself was named Gerald. Not by me—by the farmer's daughter, who fed him scraps from the table where I'd eaten breakfast that morning. I was twenty-three, spending a season at Willowbank Farm in Vermont to "reconnect with food systems," which is the kind of phrase you use when what you mean is that you're terrified of your own comfort. Gerald weighed 280 pounds, give or take. It took three bullets from a .22 rifle because I flinched the first time, and he screamed in a register I didn't think pigs could reach. We bled him, scalded him, scraped his bristles with bell scrapers that left my hands raw for days. By evening he was pork chops, but what I remember is his eye, which stayed open and fixed on nothing, and how the farmer's wife made me clear the table alone after dinner.

I don't eat pork anymore. This essay isn't about that.

What I want to argue—what I think most discussions of meat-eating carefully avoid—is that the moral question "is it wrong to eat animals?" is fundamentally malformed, and that our insistence on answering it with a simple yes or no has made us stupider about animals, not wiser. I've spent fifteen years in this argument, from farm work to academic philosophy to testifying before city councils on slaughterhouse permits. I've watched vegan friends crumble at funerals, eat salmon "just this once," rationalize the honey in their friend's birthday cake. I've watched hunters I respect describe elk as "talking to them" through the scope. The consistency we demand of each other is theological, not ethical. It serves our need for moral purity, not the animals' need for less suffering.

Consider the Buenos Aires horse sacrifice. In 2014, Argentina's Afro-Argentine religious communities won legal protection for their practice of ceremonial horse slaughter after decades of persecution by Catholic activists and secular veterinarians. The horses are killed with an axe blow, bled, and consumed in community. The Tandil chapter told me their kill rate is about twelve horses annually, on a grazing cooperative where twenty horses might die of colic or predation in any given year. Compare this to the 9 billion chickens raised in American factory farms, most of which are bred to grow so fast their legs break, living lives of such confinement that their beaks are seared off to prevent cannibalism—cannibalism being what chickens do when driven insane by proximity. I have looked into both systems. The horse sacrifice troubles our aesthetics more than our ethics should permit. The chicken nugget does the reverse.

Peter Singer's *Animal Liberation*, which I read in a canoe on the Shenandoah in 2009, convinced me that species membership is morally arbitrary, that the relevant question is capacity to suffer. This remains, I think, strictly correct and practically useless. Because what no utilitarian calculus captures is the specificity of our debts. The fishing line I inherited from my grandfather, braided Dacron, still holds bluefish I catch in Montauk waters he taught me to read for rips and baitballs. Eating those fish connects me to something perdurable in a life increasingly unmoored. Is this mere sentiment? Perhaps. But the alternative—reducing all such attachments to preference satisfaction—seems equally metaphysical, just thinner. I've watched locavore advocates in the Hudson Valley build elaborate phoniness around bone broth and "nose-to-tail" butchery classes. I've also watched vegan friends fly to Costa Rica twice yearly, their almond milk requiring millions of gallons of California water in a drought, their synthetic B12 manufactured in Chinese industrial plants. The carbon math is harder than we pretend; the suffering math is harder still.

The Danish-Swedish Farmdog at my feet as I write this, Maren, came from a breeder in Jutland who still uses her dogs for ratting in grain silos. Maren has killed perhaps forty rats, with evident joy. Is she wrong? The question is nonsensical. Not because Maren lacks moral agency in some metaphysical sense, but because predation constitutes her. To prevent her from hunting—I've tried, when rats in my Brooklyn backyard tempted me—induces a melancholy I can only anthropomorphize so far. She was bred for this. The "is it wrong?" framing assumes we can step outside our own constitution, evaluate it from nowhere. We can't. What we can do, what I think we must, is attend to the particular violence our particular lives require, refuse the comfort of ethical systems that let us off easy.

My last visit to Gerald's farm: 2019. The farmer had died; his daughter ran the operation with three Honduran workers, documented but precarious. The slaughterhouse they'd used, forty miles north, had closed after a *New York Times* expose on CO2 stunning failures—pigs regaining consciousness mid-scald, a not-uncommon industrial occurrence. She was shipping live animals to Pennsylvania now, longer transport, more stress, because local processing had become economically unviable under regulations designed partly by animal advocates. The advocates weren't wrong about the stunning. They weren't wrong about much. But the closure didn't reduce suffering; it displaced and distributed it, made it less visible to people who buy their猪肉 (pork, I force myself to name it) at Whole Foods. The daughter's name was Elena. She showed me her books, the razor margins, her father's funeral expenses still being paid. She ate meat daily. She wept about Gerald, still, fifteen years later.

I eat fish, occasionally. I eat eggs from chickens I've met. I don't eat mammals, not since Gerald, though I refuse to call this a principle. What I want from us, from the discourse, is more Elenas—more people who weep at the cost of their own living, who don't let the tears become performance or stop the killing entirely, which stopping is a luxury most humans in history haven't had. The wrong question, endlessly rehearsed. The right one, rarely asked: what does this particular animal, in this particular system, demand of me? The answer will not be consistent. Consistency is for machines, and for arguments on the internet. Life, the eating and the being eaten, is messier, more interesting, more cruel in ways that resist our beautiful formulas.
